My wife has MS, and since auto-immune diseases tend to cluster (not only in families but sometimes in the same person) she has all sorts of weird reactions to some kinds of foods. Simple carbs really send her into a tailspin (headaches, overall weakness), so she went on a ketogenic diet and it helps her a lot.

It's not my thing, but I don't have the same problems she does and I don't need to be in ketosis to keep my blood chemistry in the green.

That said, most "diets" are fads and confer few benefits over just eating a balanced diet. Many of them come with built-in nutritional pitfalls and do more harm than good for most of the people who do them. If you're going to have a highly specialized diet like keto or vegan you almost have to treat it like a job, or you may pay a price that over-rides whatever benefit you might derive from it.

The truth is that unless you have a serious medical condition that restricts what you should and should not eat, none of these specialized "diets" are necessary, or even likely to be particularly beneficial. Eat a balanced diet, eat sensible portions, don't be afraid to treat yourself in moderation, and move your body. (Any movement is better than none, so at a minimum don't be sedentary - but try to balance your exercise just like you balance your macro-nutrients... just as it's important to consume a mixture of carbs, proteins, and fats, it's also important to train a mixture of endurance, resistance, and flexibility.)
My girlfriend might have MS. Do you have any advice as a husband? Or for her?

I would recommend that she give HBOT a try, even if you have to pay for it out of your own pocket (depending on where you live, it may or may not be covered). If you're in the US, HBOT is not typically prescribed, although in some parts of the world I think it's a standard treatment. Anyway, my wife was deteriorating at an alarming rate and we brought it up to her doctor. It's not something he would have prescribed (we're in the US), and we were prepared to pay for it ourselves (it's really not that expensive anyway), but fortunately the military picked up the tab.

I don't want to give you false hope: it doesn't work for everyone, and nobody really knows why it works at all for the people who benefit from it, but in my wife's case it was nearly miraculous. Prior to her first HBOT session, if we went grocery shopping I would have to drop her off at the front door and go park because she couldn't walk very far (this was before stores started supplying scootie-puffs). At the end of her first session we walked out the clinic and kept walking for three miles... fast.

She's not cured (there is no cure), but her improvement was dramatic. It's been more than a dozen years since her diagnosis and she currently lifts weights, does yoga, and can even do some cardio (although she has to keep her intensity dialed back to a 4 or 5 on a 1-10 scale). Just a few days ago she did over 2 1/2 minutes in a planking contest with virtually no preparation - she didn't win, but she easily beat most of the other women from our gym - many of whom are half her age.

Anyway, MS treatments have come a long way since my wife was diagnosed, and there are multiple options that simply were not available then, but whatever else you do, try HBOT. Even if it doesn't work, it is extremely safe... it's just 100% Oxygen in a pressure chamber: not much different than SCUBA diving down to about 30 feet on pure O2.
